draft.title: An offence against property
card: An offence against property takes, damages or interferes with someone's property. Theft and burglary are two examples. Criminal damage is another.
Each offence has elements. The prosecution must prove every element beyond reasonable doubt. If one element is not proved, the accused is not guilty of that offence.
dishonestly taking property that belongs to another person, with the intention of permanently depriving them of it.
entering a building as a trespasser, with the intention of stealing or committing certain other offences inside. The accused does not need to take anything.
draft.remember: Property offences have elements, and the prosecution must prove every one.

a.q: Sam borrows his neighbour's ladder without asking, and plans to return it the next day. Which element of theft is most clearly missing?
opts: Intention to permanently deprive the owner of it
Property that belongs to another person
Dishonesty in how the property was taken
a.why: Theft requires an intention to permanently deprive the owner. Sam plans to return the ladder, so that element is missing. The ladder does belong to another person and Sam did take it, so those elements are present.
a.clue: Sam plans to give the ladder back.

b.q: Priya climbs through an unlocked window into a shop after closing, planning to steal stock. A guard stops her before she touches anything. Which statement is correct?
opts: She can face a burglary charge, as entry with intent counts
She cannot face a burglary charge, as nothing was taken
She can only face a theft charge, as she planned to steal
She cannot face any charge, as the window was unlocked
b.why: Burglary needs entry as a trespasser with intent to steal, and nothing needs to be taken. Priya entered the shop without permission and intended to steal, so the elements can be proved. Saying nothing was taken confuses burglary with theft.
b.clue: Does burglary need anything to be taken?

a.best: Intention to permanently deprive the owner of it

b.best: She can face a burglary charge, as entry with intent counts
